content:
The [VO2 Max Calculator](/vo2-max-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Estimate your VO2 max from age and resting heart rate — a quick fitness gauge. Enter your age, resting heart rate (bpm) and sex and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Estimate your VO2 max — the maximum rate your body can use oxygen during hard exercise — from your age and resting heart rate. It uses the Uth–Sørensen–Overgaard–Pedersen formula (VO2 max ≈ 15.3 × HRmax ÷ HRrest) with the Tanaka maximum heart rate (208 − 0.7 × age), then rates the result against published age and sex norms. This is an estimate, not a measurement: only a lab test with a mask and a treadmill or bike measures VO2 max directly, and wrist devices use their own formulas. Resting heart rate should be measured first thing in the morning, before coffee, over several days.

## How to use the VO2 Max Calculator

Start by entering your age, then entering your resting heart rate (bpm) and finally choosing your sex from the list. The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Enter your age.
2. Enter your resting heart rate — measure it lying down in the morning, before coffee.
3. Choose your sex — the rating bands differ for men and women.
4. Read the estimated VO2 max and the fitness rating.

## Formula

HRmax = 208 − 0.7 × age (Tanaka). VO2 max ≈ 15.3 × (HRmax ÷ resting heart rate). The rating compares the result with published norms for your age and sex.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [VO2 Max Calculator](/vo2-max-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. A 30-year-old man with a resting heart rate of 60: maximum heart rate is 208 − 21 = 187, and VO2 max is 15.3 × (187 ÷ 60) = 47.7 ml/kg/min — rated Excellent for men aged 30–39. Try the same figures in the [VO2 Max Calculator](/vo2-max-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Age: 30, Resting heart rate (bpm): 60, Sex: Male), the [VO2 Max Calculator](/vo2-max-calculator) returns Estimated VO2 max: 47.7 ml/kg/min, Estimated maximum heart rate: 187 bpm, Fitness rating: Excellent. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [BMI Calculator](/bmi-calculator) is worth a look before you finish.

## What VO2 max means

VO2 max is measured in millilitres of oxygen per kilogram of body weight per minute. Higher means your heart, lungs and muscles deliver and use oxygen better — it is one of the strongest single predictors of endurance performance and, in large studies, of long-term health. A sedentary adult is often in the 30s; a trained amateur runner in the 40s or 50s; elite endurance athletes reach the 70s and 80s. Because the formula uses resting heart rate, getting fitter (a lower resting rate) raises the estimate even before a lab test would show a change.

## How accurate is the estimate?

The Uth formula is one of the better field estimates, typically within about 10–15% of a lab value for most people — but it can be further off for the very fit, the very unfit, or anyone on heart-rate medication such as beta blockers, which lower resting heart rate without raising fitness. Treat the number as a trend to track over months, not a precise score. If you need an exact value — for example to set training zones — a lab test or a structured field test such as the Cooper 12-minute run is the next step.

## How to improve it

VO2 max responds to training in weeks, not years. The most effective work is a mix: two or three sessions a week of high-intensity intervals (for example 4 × 4 minutes hard with recovery) plus longer easy sessions. Losing excess weight also raises VO2 max per kilogram, because the same oxygen supply serves less body mass.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Measure resting heart rate over several mornings and use the average — one reading can be 5 bpm off.
- Do not compare your number with someone of a different age or sex — the bands exist for a reason.
- Track the trend over months; a single estimate is much less useful than the direction it moves.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is a good VO2 max?

It depends on age and sex. For men aged 30–39, above 51 is superior and 42–46 is good; for women the same age, above 43 is superior and 34–37 is good. Most untrained adults sit in the 30s. Try it with your own numbers in the [VO2 Max Calculator](/vo2-max-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### How accurate is a VO2 max estimate from resting heart rate?

Usually within about 10–15% of a lab test for most people. It is good for tracking trends and rough comparisons, but it is not a medical measurement — beta blockers and illness distort it. For figures that matter, such as money, health or legal deadlines, check the result against an authoritative source before acting on it.

### Can I improve my VO2 max?

Yes, and quickly: high-intensity interval training plus longer easy sessions typically lift it noticeably within 6–12 weeks. Losing excess weight raises it per kilogram too. Try it with your own numbers in the [VO2 Max Calculator](/vo2-max-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.
